course.title: Log Analysis
course.description: A practical, evidence-driven course for learning how to parse, normalize, search, correlate, investigate and securely handle logs across endpoints, operating systems, network sensors, web and applications, cloud services and containers. Students build toward defensible timelines, detection hypotheses, threat-hunting pivots, data-quality monitoring and reproducible evidence packages.
prerequisites: Basic networking concepts (IP, TCP/UDP, DNS, HTTP)
Basic Python is helpful for the automation sections
learningOutcomes: Parse unstructured text and structured JSONL logs into reliable fields.
Normalize heterogeneous records while retaining provenance.
Handle timestamps, time zones and bounded correlation windows correctly.
Analyze Windows, Linux, web, cloud, container, Zeek and Suricata telemetry.
Use jq, shell tools and KQL-style queries for repeatable analysis.
Correlate events and reconstruct source-linked timelines.
Write and reason about Sigma detections and ATT&CK-aligned analytics.
Identify parser failures, missing fields and telemetry gaps.
Protect logging data and produce integrity-aware evidence exports.
Complete a multi-source investigation with tested analysis tooling.

modules.title: Log Analysis Foundations
modules.description: Learn what logs represent, how source visibility works, why time semantics matter, and how logging fits into an evidence lifecycle.

lessons.title: Log Records as Evidence
lessons.description: Build a precise mental model for reading a log event as evidence rather than as a raw string.
learningObjectives: define a log record and distinguish event time from collection time
identify actor, action, object, outcome, source and context
state what a single record can and cannot prove

notes.text: A log record is an observation emitted by a system, application, service, sensor, or control. Analysis turns that observation into a defensible claim by preserving context and uncertainty.

items: Event time describes when the source says the event occurred; observed or ingest time may be later.
Severity is a prioritization field, not proof of maliciousness.
A record becomes more useful when identity, host, process, network and outcome are available.

quiz.question: Which timestamp most directly represents when the source says the event occurred?
quiz.explanation: The event timestamp is associated with the occurrence; ingest can happen later.

summary: Logs are evidence with provenance and uncertainty.
A single event should usually be treated as a pivot, not a verdict.

lessons.title: Log Sources and Visibility
lessons.description: Map endpoint, identity, application, network, cloud and security-control sources to investigative questions.
learningObjectives: select complementary sources for an investigation
identify blind spots caused by missing telemetry

items: Endpoint logs can expose process, service, file and authentication activity.
Network logs expose relationships and protocol metadata.
Application logs often contain business actions unavailable elsewhere.
Identity and cloud audit logs can be authoritative for account and control-plane operations.

summary: Source selection should follow the investigative question.
No single source gives complete visibility.

lessons.title: Time Semantics and Clock Drift
lessons.description: Build trustworthy time handling for multi-source timelines.
learningObjectives: explain clock drift and ingestion latency

notes.text:
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
s = "2026-09-07T19:30:00+05:30"
dt = datetime.fromisoformat(s)
print(dt.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")).isoformat())
Do not silently interpret a naive timestamp as local time. Unknown timezone context is an analytical limitation.

summary: Normalize for comparison, retain originals for auditability.
A timeline is an ordered reconstruction, not automatically a perfect clock order.

lessons.title: Syslog and Structured Logging
lessons.description: Read RFC 5424 structure and recognize where older BSD syslog conventions differ.
learningObjectives: distinguish structured data from free-form message text
recognize the legacy role of RFC 3164

notes.text: <34>1 2026-09-07T14:15:00Z host sshd 1234 ID47 [meta@32473 iut="3"] Failed password
RFC 5424 defines a standardized syslog message format. RFC 3164 documents observed BSD syslog behavior and is informational rather than a modern Internet Standard.

summary: Use structure-aware parsing when possible.
Know which source conventions are strict format rules and which are historical practice.

lessons.title: Log Management Lifecycle
lessons.description: Connect collection, transport, storage, analysis, retention and disposal into one operational lifecycle.
learningObjectives: identify failure points from source to analyst
explain why retention and integrity affect investigations

items: Collection determines what evidence exists.
Transport can introduce loss, duplication or delay.
Storage must support search, retention and appropriate access.
Disposal should follow documented requirements.

summary: Logging is an operational system, not just a file.
A lost or untrusted record cannot be recovered by better querying later.

tasks.title: Normalize Mixed Authentication Records
tasks.description: Normalize two differently shaped authentication records into one canonical structure.
tasks.problemStatement: Parse one key=value record and one JSON record and emit timestamp, user, source_ip, action and outcome fields.
tasks.hint: Parse each format separately, then map to a common dictionary.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Each parser understands its own field names while emitting the same analytical vocabulary.

modules.title: Parsing and Extraction
modules.description: Convert unstructured and structured records into fields using Python, regex, shell tools and jq.

lessons.title: Parsing Key=Value and Semi-Structured Text
lessons.description: Extract fields from semi-structured messages while preserving raw records.
learningObjectives: use bounded parsing rather than greedy matching
retain the raw record for replay

notes.text:
import re
line = "Failed login user=alice src=203.0.113.10 service=ssh"
m = re.search(r"user=(\S+)\s+src=(\S+)\s+service=(\S+)", line)
print(m.groupdict() if m else None)

practicals.title: Parse Mixed Authentication Inputs
practicals.description: Build canonical JSONL records from one KV line and one JSON record.
steps: Create sample KV and JSON input.
Implement source-specific parsers.
Validate timestamps and output common fields.
Retain a source_format field.
practicals.output: Canonical records containing timestamp, user, source_ip, action, outcome and source_format.

summary: Identify the source grammar before writing a parser.
Prefer explicit field boundaries and named groups.

lessons.title: JSONL and Structured Records
lessons.description: Process line-oriented JSON safely and distinguish syntax validity from semantic validity.
summary: JSONL supports streaming because each line is an independent JSON value.
A valid JSON document can still have wrong types, missing fields or invalid timestamps.

lessons.title: Regex for Extraction and Detection
lessons.description: Use regular expressions precisely without making detection logic unreadable.
learningObjectives: use anchors, groups and bounded quantifiers

notes.text:
import re
pat = re.compile(r"(?P<user>[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)@(?P<domain>[A-Za-z0-9.-]+)")
m = pat.search("login for alice@example.org")
print(m.groupdict()) if m else None

summary: Regex should reduce ambiguity, not conceal it.
A formal parser is preferable when the source has a stable grammar.

lessons.title: Shell Analysis with grep and awk
lessons.description: Build fast, reproducible command-line investigations over text streams.
learningObjectives: aggregate values with sort and uniq

notes.text: grep "Failed login" auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

summary: Use shell pipelines for focused inspection.
Save important or complex commands so the analysis can be reproduced.

lessons.title: jq for JSON Logs
lessons.description: Use structure-aware querying for JSON security logs.

notes.text: jq 'select(.event.outcome=="failure") | {ts:.timestamp, user:.user.name, ip:.source.ip}' events.jsonl

summary: Use jq rather than substring matching when the source is JSON.
Keep filters small and composable.

lessons.title: Schema Validation and Parser Testing
lessons.description: Turn parsing into tested software so schema drift is detected rather than silently absorbed.

items: Test missing keys, nulls, changed separators and invalid timestamps.
Keep raw input available so a parser change can be replayed.
Treat parser errors as data-quality events with monitoring.

summary: Parser failures can become security blind spots.
Automated tests should fail when the source grammar changes unexpectedly.

tasks.title: Detect an Authentication Failure Burst
tasks.description: Identify sources with repeated failures in a bounded window.
tasks.problemStatement: Report any source IP with at least three failures within five minutes.
tasks.hint: Sort timestamps by source and use a two-pointer window.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The window includes the full five-minute interval and moves its left edge only when necessary.

modules.title: Normalization and Data Quality
modules.description: Normalize heterogeneous data, preserve provenance, enrich carefully and quantify data quality.

lessons.title: Canonical Fields and Schema Mapping
lessons.description: Create a shared vocabulary across unlike log sources.
learningObjectives: map source-specific fields to canonical names
explain the value of ECS and OpenTelemetry semantics

notes.text:
event = {
  "@timestamp":"2026-09-07T14:15:00Z",
  "user.name":"alice",
  "source.ip":"203.0.113.10",
  "event.action":"login",
  "event.outcome":"failure"
}

summary: Normalization translates meaning; it should not erase original evidence.
Use established semantic models when practical instead of inventing inconsistent aliases.

lessons.title: Deduplication and Event Identity
lessons.description: Prevent double-counting while avoiding destructive deduplication.
learningObjectives: explain when identical events are legitimately repeated

items: Stable producer event IDs are preferable to constructed fingerprints.
Fallback fingerprints can use source, timestamp, host and message but have collision risks.
Repeated authentication failures may be distinct events even when message text matches.

summary: Deduplicate only when source semantics support it.
Keep enough provenance to explain why records were merged.

lessons.title: Enrichment with Identity and Asset Context
lessons.description: Add context that helps the analyst interpret who and what generated an event.
learningObjectives: enrich with user and asset metadata

items: Identity enrichment can map an account to role or ownership.
Asset enrichment can classify host roles.
Threat-intelligence and DNS enrichment should carry source and freshness context.

summary: Enrichment raises analytical value but introduces staleness and dependency risks.
Keep original source fields separate from derived context.

lessons.title: Data Quality and Missingness
lessons.description: Measure data quality before making strong conclusions.
learningObjectives: distinguish missing, null and placeholder values
treat missingness as evidence of a telemetry limitation

notes.text:
required = ["timestamp", "event_type", "source_ip"]
missing = [f for f in required if not event.get(f)]
print(missing)

summary: Data quality is part of detection quality.
Unknown should not be confused with not-applicable or not-collected.

lessons.title: Retention, Integrity and Access
lessons.description: Understand how logs remain useful as evidence over time.

items: Retention supports historical investigations but increases storage and privacy costs.
Raw logs should be protected from unauthorized modification.
Administrative access to logs should itself be auditable.

summary: The value of logs depends on availability, trustworthiness and appropriate access.
Retention should be driven by documented risk and requirements.

tasks.title: Merge Evidence into a Timeline
tasks.description: Merge two differently shaped JSONL sources into one chronological evidence timeline.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a timeline that preserves source identity and normalized time.
tasks.hint: Use source-specific parsing functions and a common event structure.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The combined list uses a consistent timestamp type and retains the source label for each event.

modules.title: Host and OS Log Analysis
modules.description: Investigate Windows and Linux authentication, process, service and system evidence.

lessons.title: Windows Authentication Events
lessons.description: Analyze Windows authentication events with contextual pivots.
learningObjectives: interpret Event IDs 4624 and 4625 at a high level
use account, source address and logon context as pivots
avoid concluding compromise from a single event

items: 4624 records a successful account logon; 4625 records a failed logon.
Logon type, account, source address and workstation context can change interpretation.
Correlate with adjacent process, network and account-management events.

summary: Event IDs are pivots, not verdicts.
Always validate whether the behavior fits the asset and user context.

lessons.title: Windows Process Creation and Services
lessons.description: Use process and service installation events for endpoint pivots.
learningObjectives: explain the value of command-line and parent context
use Event 7045 as a service-installation pivot

items: Event 4688 can record process creation when the relevant audit policy is configured.
Command line and parent process context help distinguish expected activity from suspicious execution.
Service installation may be legitimate administration or persistence; validate against change context.

summary: Endpoint evidence is strongest as a chain: user → parent → process → network/file/service activity.

lessons.title: Linux journalctl
lessons.description: Query systemd journal data using narrow, explicit filters.
learningObjectives: filter journal entries by unit and time

notes.text:
journalctl --since "2026-09-07 14:00:00" --until "2026-09-07 15:00:00" -u sshd
journalctl -p warning..alert --since today

summary: Start narrow and widen the window only when evidence requires it.
Record commands and time ranges for reproducibility.

lessons.title: Linux Authentication and Audit Evidence
lessons.description: Correlate authentication records with privileged actions and audit telemetry.

items: Authentication log paths and formats vary by distribution and configuration.
auditd produces security-audit records distinct from ordinary application messages.
Correlate identity with process, privilege and file evidence where available.

summary: Linux logging is configuration-dependent.
A missing log source must be reported as a limitation, not ignored.

tasks.title: Extract Suricata Alerts with jq
tasks.description: Extract alert evidence from EVE JSON without treating JSON as raw text.
tasks.problemStatement: Print timestamp, source, destination and signature for alert records.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The filter uses the JSON structure and preserves the nested alert semantics.

modules.title: Network Log Analysis
modules.description: Analyze Zeek and Suricata telemetry and reason about network context, metadata and baselines.

lessons.title: Zeek conn.log
lessons.description: Use Zeek connection records to reconstruct network relationships.
learningObjectives: group connections by source and destination

items: Zeek conn.log records TCP, UDP and ICMP connection metadata.
Connection records support relationship and timing questions.
Metadata may not expose application payload, especially for encrypted protocols.

summary: Connection logs are strong for relationships, not full content visibility.

lessons.title: Zeek DNS, HTTP and TLS Metadata
lessons.description: Use protocol-specific logs for pivots and anomaly analysis.
learningObjectives: pivot from DNS names to hosts

items: DNS can expose queried names and response context.
Zeek HTTP logging is less active for end-to-end encrypted HTTPS unless visibility is otherwise provided.
TLS metadata can still support endpoint and timing analysis.

summary: Protocol metadata often remains useful even when payloads are unavailable.

lessons.title: Suricata EVE JSON
lessons.description: Read IDS/IPS output as a stream of typed JSON events.
learningObjectives: distinguish Suricata alert records from other EVE event types
correlate an alert with flow and protocol records

notes.text: jq 'select(.event_type=="alert") | {timestamp, src:.src_ip, dst:.dest_ip, signature:.alert.signature}' eve.json

practicals.title: Extract and Pivot Network Alerts
practicals.description: Use jq and simple Python aggregation to inspect Suricata and connection evidence.
steps: Extract Suricata alerts with jq.
Count connections by source.
Pivot from alert source IP into connection records.
Record the exact filters used.
practicals.solution:
jq 'select(.event_type=="alert") | {timestamp,src:.src_ip,dst:.dest_ip,signature:.alert.signature}' eve.json
python - <<'PY'
import json
from collections import Counter
c=Counter()
with open('conn.jsonl',encoding='utf-8') as f:
    for line in f: c[json.loads(line)['src_ip']]+=1
print(c)
PY
practicals.output: Alert field output plus per-source connection counts suitable for further pivots.

summary: An alert is evidence that a detection rule matched telemetry; it is not automatically proof that a payload succeeded.

lessons.title: Ports, Services and Network Context
lessons.description: Use IANA and endpoint context without assuming port number equals protocol identity.
learningObjectives: use IANA as a service-name reference
validate service identity with stronger evidence when available

notes.text: IANA maintains the service-name and port-number registry. A port number is a hint, not conclusive proof of the application protocol because software can listen on non-standard ports and proxies can change apparent endpoints.

summary: Validate unexpected services using process, protocol or asset context.

resources.title: IANA Service Names and Port Numbers

lessons.title: Network Baselines and Rare Behavior
lessons.description: Create simple behavioral baselines and interpret outliers carefully.

notes.text:
from collections import Counter
ports=[443,443,53,22,443,8080]
print(Counter(ports).most_common())

summary: Rare activity creates candidates for investigation.
Segment baselines by role and time when justified.

tasks.title: Write a KQL Authentication Pivot
tasks.description: Find sources that have both failures and a later success in a bounded interval.
tasks.problemStatement: Build a KQL query for a five-minute authentication investigation window.
tasks.hint: Create filtered datasets and join or summarize on SourceIP.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The query keeps the correlation window explicit and exposes the timestamps needed for validation.

modules.title: Application, Web, Cloud and Container Logs
modules.description: Extend log analysis into distributed application, web, cloud and Kubernetes environments.

lessons.title: Web Access Logs
lessons.description: Analyze web request logs for probing, abuse and errors.
learningObjectives: parse source IP, method, URI and status
distinguish server response from security outcome

notes.text:
log = '203.0.113.10 - - [07/Sep/2026:14:20:00 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 404 512'
import re
m=re.match(r'(?P<ip>\S+) .* "\S+ (?P<uri>\S+) HTTP/[^"]+" (?P<status>\d+)',log)
print(m.groupdict())

summary: 404/403/5xx patterns need contextual interpretation.
Combine web data with authentication and application logs.

lessons.title: Application and API Logs
lessons.description: Use business-level context and correlation IDs to follow actions across services.
learningObjectives: trace a request using a correlation ID
avoid logging secrets or unnecessary sensitive data

items: Business events such as role changes or exports may exist only in application logs.
Correlation IDs link gateway and service records.
OWASP recommends excluding sensitive authentication material and protecting log access.

summary: Application logs can explain the business action that infrastructure logs merely hint at.

lessons.title: Cloud Audit Logs
lessons.description: Analyze cloud control-plane records using principal, action and resource context.
learningObjectives: pivot from principal to action and resource
keep account/project/subscription and region in scope
separate control-plane context from workload events

items: Cloud audit records commonly include actor/principal, API action, resource, result and source context.
Scope boundaries matter because the same user identity can operate across accounts or subscriptions.
Correlate cloud control-plane records with endpoint and application evidence when possible.

summary: Cloud logs require explicit account and tenant scope.

lessons.title: Kubernetes and Container Logs
lessons.description: Analyze ephemeral workloads with workload and orchestration context.
learningObjectives: differentiate application container logs from audit events
correlate pod, namespace and node context

items: Container stdout/stderr is different from Kubernetes API audit activity.
Workloads can move or restart, so pod identity and lifecycle context matter.
Centralized collection is especially important for ephemeral resources.

summary: Do not assume a pod name is a durable host identity.

tasks.title: Create a Sigma Authentication Rule
tasks.description: Write a portable event-level detection for authentication failures.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a valid Sigma-style YAML rule with metadata, logsource, detection and false-positive guidance.
tasks.hint: Keep the semantics generic and document backend mapping assumptions.
tasks.solutionCode:
title: Authentication Failure Review
id: 44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444
status: experimental
description: Detects authentication failure events for analyst review.
logsource:
  category: authentication
detection:
  selection:
    outcome: failure
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - User mistakes
level: low
tasks.solutionExplanation: The rule is event-level and can be extended with correlation or thresholding appropriate to the target backend.

modules.title: Correlation and Timeline Analysis
modules.description: Join evidence across systems, reason with bounded time windows and reconstruct multi-step event sequences.

lessons.title: Correlation Keys and Joins
lessons.description: Build cross-source joins using strong identifiers and bounded fallback keys.

items: Useful keys include event IDs, request IDs, user, host, process ID, source IP and time.
Weak joins should combine multiple fields and a narrow time window.
Document the key and scope used for reproducibility.

summary: Correlation is hypothesis building, not automatic truth.

lessons.title: Time-Window Correlation
lessons.description: Detect related activity without requiring exact timestamp equality.
learningObjectives: account for clock skew and ingestion delay

notes.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
base=datetime.fromisoformat("2026-09-07T14:00:00+00:00")
for minutes in (2,8):
    ts=base+timedelta(minutes=minutes)
    print(minutes, ts-base <= timedelta(minutes=5))

summary: Wider windows increase recall and can increase false correlations.
Choose the smallest window justified by system behavior.

lessons.title: Timeline Reconstruction
lessons.description: Create evidence-linked timelines and label uncertainty.
learningObjectives: merge heterogeneous events into a canonical timeline

items: A useful timeline carries timestamp, source, actor, action, outcome and evidence reference.
Gaps should be visible rather than silently filled.
Precision should not exceed the source precision.

practicals.title: Reconstruct a Cross-Source Timeline
practicals.description: Merge authentication and endpoint logs into a source-linked UTC timeline.
steps: Prepare two JSONL files with different field names.
Normalize each source into a shared structure.
Sort by normalized event time.
Review gaps and provenance.
practicals.output: A chronological timeline with normalized timestamps and source labels.

summary: A good timeline makes multiple sources understandable without hiding uncertainty.

lessons.title: Sequence Detection
lessons.description: Model multi-step behaviors as explicit state transitions.

notes.text:
events=["login_failure","login_failure","login_success","privilege_change"]
pattern=["login_failure","login_success","privilege_change"]
i=0
for e in events:
    if i<len(pattern) and e==pattern[i]: i+=1
print(i==len(pattern))

summary: Sequence detection makes assumptions about ordering and allowable gaps explicit.
A sequence match should trigger investigation, not automatic attribution.

tasks.title: Measure Parser Completeness
tasks.description: Report missing rates for required fields in a JSONL source.
tasks.problemStatement: Calculate how many records miss each required field and the percentage of the dataset affected.
tasks.hint: Count records and missing occurrences in one pass.
tasks.solutionExplanation: This produces a measurable data-quality report instead of silently discarding malformed data.

modules.title: SIEM Search and KQL
modules.description: Use KQL-style querying for investigation, aggregation, extraction, correlation and query optimization.

lessons.title: KQL Query Structure
lessons.description: Use the Kusto pipeline model to filter, project, sort and summarize log data.

notes.text:
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID in (4624,4625)
| summarize Count=count() by Account, EventID
| order by Count desc

quiz.question: Which KQL operator filters records?
quiz.explanation: `where` evaluates a predicate and keeps matching records.

summary: Start with time bounds.
Filter early and project only the columns needed for the question.

lessons.title: KQL String Extraction
lessons.description: Turn unstructured log fields into queryable values with KQL extraction functions.
learningObjectives: avoid repeated expensive parsing when upstream normalization is available

notes.text:
MyLogs
| extend User = extract(@"user=([^ ]+)", 1, RawMessage)
| where isnotempty(User)
| summarize Events=count() by User

summary: Extraction is useful for legacy unstructured sources.
Durable normalization can be preferable when the same field is queried repeatedly.

lessons.title: KQL Aggregation and Joins
lessons.description: Move from row-by-row inspection to population analysis.
learningObjectives: aggregate by user, host or IP

notes.text:
let failures = AuthLogs
| where Outcome == "failure"
| summarize Failures=count() by SourceIP;
failures
| top 20 by Failures desc

summary: Aggregations reveal distributions and outliers.
Joins should use intentional keys and bounded populations.

lessons.title: Search Design and Query Performance
lessons.description: Design searches that are correct, explainable and economical.
learningObjectives: separate exploratory searches from production analytics

items: Time bounding is a correctness and performance control.
Keep exploratory queries readable enough to validate their semantics.
Document assumptions, exclusions and data sources before deploying a query as a detection.

summary: A fast query that answers the wrong question is still wrong.

tasks.title: Build a Rare-Port Baseline
tasks.description: Summarize destination-port frequency by host and identify rare values.
tasks.problemStatement: Flag ports used fewer than three times by each source host.
tasks.hint: Use nested counters keyed by source host and destination port.
tasks.solutionCode:
import json
from collections import defaultdict,Counter
c=defaultdict(Counter)
with open("conn.jsonl",encoding="utf-8") as f:
 for line in f:
  e=json.loads(line); c[e["src_ip"]][int(e["dest_port"])]+=1
for host,ports in c.items(): print(host,[p for p,n in ports.items() if n<3])
tasks.solutionExplanation: The result is a candidate baseline. Rare does not imply malicious.

modules.title: Detection Engineering and Hunting
modules.description: Turn log observations into detections, Sigma rules, hunts and disciplined triage decisions.

lessons.title: Detection Hypotheses
lessons.description: Translate an analytical observation into explicit detection logic.

items: A useful detection states the suspicious behavior, evidence source, scope and known benign explanations.
Thresholds and windows are assumptions that must be tested.
Every detection should have a validation and tuning plan.

summary: Detection quality depends on telemetry quality and context.

lessons.title: Sigma Rules
lessons.description: Create portable YAML detections and document their operational context.

notes.text:
title: Authentication Failure Review
id: 33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333
status: experimental
description: Detects authentication failure events for investigation.
logsource:
  category: authentication
detection:
  selection:
    outcome: failure
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - User mistakes
level: low

quiz.question: Which Sigma sections define the source and matching logic?
quiz.explanation: `logsource` identifies the event source and `detection` specifies matching logic.

summary: Sigma is a portable detection format; backend field mapping still matters.
Good rules document scope, intent and false positives.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting from Logs
lessons.description: Perform hypothesis-driven searches for behavior that did not trigger an alert.

items: Start with a behavior hypothesis, not a random search.
Use users, hosts, processes, IPs, domains and timestamps as pivots.
A negative result is meaningful only when telemetry coverage is understood.

practicals.title: Write and Review a Sigma Rule
practicals.description: Author an event-level Sigma rule and evaluate its assumptions.
steps: Choose an authentication log source.
Define the behavior the rule matches.
Add false-positive guidance.
Review whether fields exist in the target schema.
practicals.solution:
title: Authentication Failure Review
id: 44444444-4444-4444-8444-444444444444
status: experimental
description: Detects authentication failure events for analyst review.
logsource:
  category: authentication
detection:
  selection:
    outcome: failure
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - User mistakes
level: low
practicals.output: A portable detection rule with explicit source assumptions and false positives.

summary: Hunting is iterative: hypothesis → query → evidence → refinement → conclusion.

lessons.title: ATT&CK Mapping for Log Evidence
lessons.description: Map observed behavior to ATT&CK concepts without turning the framework into an attribution engine.
learningObjectives: use ATT&CK to organize behaviors and analytics

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK deprecated the legacy data-source model for new additions in v18 and is moving toward more specific data-component and detection-analytics concepts. Legacy data-source pages remain useful for reference.

summary: ATT&CK describes adversary behavior; it does not prove actor identity.

lessons.title: Alert Triage and Tuning
lessons.description: Turn a detection match into a consistent analyst decision and improve signal quality.

items: Pivot from the alert into adjacent telemetry.
Check expected asset, user and time context.
Prefer narrow exclusions over broad suppression.

summary: Triage is evidence gathering under time pressure.
Good tuning lowers noise without deleting the behavior of interest.

tasks.title: Build an Evidence Manifest
tasks.description: Create a manifest containing SHA-256 hashes and metadata for exported log evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Write a JSON manifest with file path, size, hash and generation timestamp.
tasks.hint: Hash in bounded chunks rather than loading the whole file into memory.
tasks.solutionCode:
import hashlib,json
from datetime import datetime,timezone
from pathlib import Path
p=Path("events.jsonl"); h=hashlib.sha256()
with open(p,"rb") as f:
 for chunk in iter(lambda:f.read(1024*1024),b""): h.update(chunk)
manifest={"generated_at":datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),"files":[{"name":str(p),"size":p.stat().st_size,"sha256":h.hexdigest()}]}
Path("manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2),encoding="utf-8")
print(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The manifest documents the analyzed copy and gives a reproducible integrity value.

modules.title: Investigation Workflows
modules.description: Apply log analysis to authentication, web, endpoint and DNS investigations and produce reproducible evidence packages.

lessons.title: Authentication Investigation
lessons.description: Investigate account activity from the initial event through corroborating evidence.
learningObjectives: pivot on account, device and source

items: Review failures, successes, source addresses and authentication methods.
Pivot from account to endpoint, VPN or cloud events where available.
Do not declare credential compromise from one anomaly alone.

summary: Authentication investigation is a correlation problem, not an Event-ID lookup.

lessons.title: Web Attack Investigation
lessons.description: Correlate web, application and detection logs to assess suspected web abuse.

items: Pivot on source IP, URI, request ID, identity and response status.
Correlate errors with application exceptions and downstream actions.
A successful HTTP response is not itself proof of a sensitive action succeeding.

summary: Layered correlation is what distinguishes reconnaissance from confirmed impact.

lessons.title: Endpoint Process Investigation
lessons.description: Use process trees, users, command lines and network pivots to assess suspicious execution.
learningObjectives: correlate process with user and network evidence

items: Command-line data can be highly useful but may be absent or truncated.
Parent-child context is more informative than a process name alone.
Network connections near process start can provide strong pivots.

summary: Process investigation works best as a chain of related evidence.

lessons.title: DNS and Beaconing Investigation
lessons.description: Use DNS and network metadata to test suspicious-domain and periodic-communication hypotheses.

items: Periodicity is interesting but not unique to command-and-control.
Validate domain context with trustworthy enrichment.
Correlate DNS with processes and connections.

summary: Behavioral signals become stronger when alternate explanations are tested.

lessons.title: Evidence Packages and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Produce a concise, source-linked package another analyst can reproduce.
learningObjectives: record query scope and time bounds

items: Each major claim should point to source records or query output.
Record data-source limitations.
A useful report includes summary, timeline, evidence, interpretation, confidence and next actions.

summary: Reproducibility is a quality property of investigation work.

tasks.title: Triage a Multi-Source Authentication Case
tasks.description: Use a successful login as an anchor and pivot across related evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Find nearby events sharing the user, host or source IP and report the evidence chain.
tasks.hint: Start with the anchor event, then widen to user/host/IP pivots within a fixed window.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The pivot is intentionally evidence-focused and leaves the final maliciousness decision to the analyst.

modules.title: Scale, Security and Evidence Handling
modules.description: Handle production-scale constraints, telemetry health, secure logging, modern semantic models and integrity-aware evidence export.

lessons.title: Volume, Cardinality and Retention Tiers
lessons.description: Reason about field choices, volume and retention without sacrificing investigation value.

items: High-cardinality fields can increase storage and query cost.
Summaries can reduce repetitive query work but should not replace required raw evidence.
Retention tiers should reflect investigative and business requirements.

summary: Cost optimization must not silently remove fields needed for future investigations.

lessons.title: Telemetry Health and Pipeline Monitoring
lessons.description: Detect broken collection before it creates an invisible security gap.
learningObjectives: define health indicators for critical sources

items: Useful health signals include last-seen time, event rate, parser error rate and volume anomalies.
A sudden drop in logs can indicate failure or interference.
Health monitoring should remain visible when a monitored pipeline fails.

summary: Detection availability depends on telemetry availability.

lessons.title: Secure Logging and Sensitive Data
lessons.description: Protect log confidentiality and integrity while preserving enough detail for analysis.
learningObjectives: identify secrets that should not be logged
recognize log injection and unsafe message handling

items: OWASP recommends excluding sensitive authentication material from logs.
Structured logging reduces ambiguity and injection risk.
Logs may contain sensitive infrastructure and identity data and should be protected accordingly.

summary: Logging creates another security-sensitive data store; design it intentionally.

lessons.title: OpenTelemetry Log Model
lessons.description: Understand modern semantic log models and mapping from legacy sources.
learningObjectives: describe LogRecord timestamps, body, resource and attributes
map legacy records conceptually into a common model

notes.text: OpenTelemetry defines a stable Logs Data Model intended to provide common semantics across system, third-party and first-party application logs. It distinguishes event timestamp from observed timestamp and provides resource and attribute concepts.

practicals.title: Generate an Evidence Manifest
practicals.description: Create a SHA-256 manifest for a bounded log export.
steps: Select an evidence file.
Hash it in chunks.
Record size and UTC generation time.
Write JSON and verify the hash again.
practicals.solution:
import hashlib,json
from datetime import datetime,timezone
from pathlib import Path
p=Path("events.jsonl"); h=hashlib.sha256()
with open(p,"rb") as f:
 for chunk in iter(lambda:f.read(1024*1024),b""): h.update(chunk)
manifest={"generated_at":datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),"files":[{"name":str(p),"size":p.stat().st_size,"sha256":h.hexdigest()}]}
Path("manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2),encoding="utf-8")
print(json.dumps(manifest,indent=2))
practicals.output: A JSON manifest containing file identity, size, generation time and SHA-256 hash.

summary: Semantic models allow tools to agree on meaning while original formats remain diverse.

lessons.title: Evidence Export and Integrity
lessons.description: Export bounded log subsets while preserving analysis context and file integrity.
learningObjectives: compute SHA-256 hashes for exported files
summary: Hashing demonstrates integrity of an exported copy after collection; it does not prove the source itself was trustworthy.

modules.title: Final Project: Cross-Source Log Investigation Toolkit
modules.description: Apply the complete log-analysis workflow to a reproducible multi-source investigation.

lessons.title: Project Architecture and Evidence Flow
lessons.description: Plan the capstone before implementation and identify where validation, normalization, correlation and integrity fit.
learningObjectives: define tests for the key analytical behavior

items: Input: source-specific JSONL evidence.
Processing: parse → validate → normalize → correlate → report.
Integrity: hashes accompany exported evidence.
Testing: timestamp rejection and burst detection are unit-tested.

summary: The capstone is modular so every transformation can be inspected.
Data-quality failures are reported instead of silently hidden.

project.name: Cross-Source Log Investigation Toolkit
project.description: A reproducible Python CLI that ingests authentication, endpoint and network JSONL evidence, validates required fields, normalizes time, reconstructs a source-linked timeline, detects a bounded authentication-failure burst followed by success, and produces an integrity manifest and limitations section.
steps: Prepare synthetic auth.jsonl, endpoint.jsonl and network.jsonl evidence.
Validate required fields and timestamps before analysis.
Merge valid events into a UTC-normalized timeline.
Detect repeated authentication failures from one source within five minutes and check for a later success.
Generate a report separating findings from limitations.
Generate SHA-256 hashes for the exported evidence inputs.
Run the unit tests and preserve the exact query/input scope used.

files.test_analyze_logs.py:
import unittest
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from analyze_logs import parse_ts, find_auth_bursts

class TestAnalysis(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_naive_timestamp_rejected(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError): parse_ts("2026-09-07T14:00:00")
    def test_burst_and_later_success(self):
        base=datetime(2026,9,7,14,0,tzinfo=timezone.utc)
        ev=[]
        from datetime import timedelta
        for i in [0,1,2]:
            ev.append({"_event_time":base+timedelta(minutes=i),"event_type":"auth","source_ip":"203.0.113.5","outcome":"failure"})
        ev.append({"_event_time":base+timedelta(minutes=4),"event_type":"auth","source_ip":"203.0.113.5","outcome":"success"})
        f=find_auth_bursts(ev)
        self.assertEqual(f[0]["failure_count"],3)
        self.assertEqual(f[0]["later_successes"],1)
if __name__ == '__main__': unittest.main()

project.explanation: The toolkit is intentionally standard-library based so students can inspect each transformation. It rejects naive timestamps, reports schema problems rather than dropping them silently, keeps source and line provenance, uses a bounded rolling-window detector, and hashes evidence copies. The report explicitly states limitations so a rule match is not mistaken for proof of compromise.
